items.title: The Five Noble Knowledges: How a Noble One Verifies His Own Concentration

items.zh: 謂我此三摩地，是聖、無染、無執，廣說如經。此中示現五行相智。謂自體智、補特伽羅智、清淨智、果智、入出定相智。聖者，善故名聖；又無漏故名聖。無染者，顯善聖性。無執者，顯無漏聖性。非凡夫所近者，謂諸佛及聖弟子所親近故。是聰叡所讚者，謂即彼所稱讚故。是諸聰叡同梵行者常不呵毀者，謂一切時常稱讚故。非如世間初靜慮等，為背下地修方便故，先以靜相而稱讚之；為趣上地修方便故，後以麁相而復呵毀。
items.en: "This concentration of mine is noble, undefiled, ungrasping," and so on as the scripture explains at length. Herein five aspect-knowledges are displayed: self-nature knowledge, person knowledge, purity knowledge, fruit knowledge, and entering-and-exiting knowledge. "Noble": because wholesome it is called noble, and because uncontaminated it is called noble. "Undefiled" shows its wholesome noble nature; "ungrasping" shows its uncontaminated noble nature. "Not resorted to by ordinary beings" — because the buddhas and the noble disciples have intimately attained it. "Praised by the wise" — because they extol it. "Never censured by the wise, one's fellow practitioners" — because at all times they praise it — unlike the worldly first dhyāna and the rest, which, to turn away from the lower ground, one first praises by its calm mark, and then, to advance to the higher ground, censures by its coarse mark.

items.zh: 寂靜者，所治煩惱永寂靜故。微妙者，自地煩惱不愛味故。得安隱道者，所得之道無退轉故。證心一趣者，已得無尋無伺地故。現在安樂者，能得現法樂住故。後樂異熟者，引無餘依涅槃樂故。正念而入者，善取能入三摩地相，無忘失故。正念而出者，善取能出三摩地相，無忘失故。
items.en: "Quiescent" — because the afflictions it counters are forever stilled. "Subtle" — because there is no relish for its own ground's afflictions. "Attaining a secure path" — because the path attained does not retrogress. "Realising the mind's single course" — because one has reached the ground with neither applied nor sustained thought. "Present ease" — because it can win the pleasant abiding in this very life. "Future blissful ripening" — because it draws forth the bliss of nirvāṇa-without-remainder. "Mindfully entering" — because one firmly grasps, without forgetting, the mark by which one enters the concentration. "Mindfully exiting" — because one firmly grasps, without forgetting, the mark by which one emerges from it.

items.title: The Noble Five-Limb Concentration (First Limb): The Body Drenched in the First Dhyāna's Bliss

items.zh: 復次，云何聖五支三摩地？謂諸苾芻，即此身內離生喜樂，廣說如經。離生喜樂者，謂初靜慮地所攝喜樂。所滋潤者，謂喜所潤。遍滋潤者，謂樂所潤。遍充滿者，謂加行究竟作意位。遍適悅者，謂在已前諸作意位。由彼位中，亦有喜樂時時間起，然非久住，亦不圓滿。於此身中無有少分而不充滿者，謂在加行究竟果作意位。
items.en: Furthermore, what is the noble five-limb concentration? Monks who, within this very body, [experience] the joy-and-bliss born of seclusion, as the scripture explains at length. "Joy-and-bliss born of seclusion" is the joy-and-bliss included in the first-dhyāna ground. "Drenched" means moistened by joy; "pervadingly drenched" means moistened by bliss. "Wholly filled" refers to the consummation-of-means attention; "pervadingly gladdened" refers to the earlier attention-stages, in which joy and bliss also arise from time to time, but do not last and are not complete. "Not the least part of the body left unfilled" refers to the fruit-of-the-consummation-of-means attention.

items.zh: 譬如黠慧能沐浴人，或彼弟子者，當知喻於修觀行者。銅器、瓦器、或蜯蛤器者，喻為離欲生喜樂故，教授教誡。細沐浴末者，喻能順彼出離尋等。水澆灌者：當知喻於尋清淨道。沐浴摶者，以喻於身。帶津膩者，喻喜和合。膩所隨者，喻樂和合。遍內外者，喻無間隙喜樂和合。不強者，喻無散動。
items.en: The skilled bath-attendant, or his pupil, should be known to illustrate the practitioner of contemplation. The copper, clay, or shell vessel illustrates the instruction and admonition [given] for the sake of the joy-and-bliss born of leaving desire. The fine bath-powder illustrates what conforms to the applied thought of renunciation and the rest. The water poured over it should be known to illustrate the purifying path of applied thought. The kneaded ball of bath-powder illustrates the body. Its being moist and greasy illustrates the union of joy; its being suffused with grease illustrates the union of bliss; its being so throughout, within and without, illustrates the seamless union of joy and bliss. Its not being stiff illustrates the absence of scattering and disturbance.

items.zh: 不弱者，喻無染污，亦無愛味。
items.en: Its not being weak illustrates that it is undefiled and free from relishing.

items.title: The Second, Third, and Fourth Limbs: The Same Bliss, Varied by Dhyāna

items.zh: 又於第二喻有差別。山者，喻於無尋伺定。尖頂者，喻於第二靜慮無尋無伺，於所緣境一味勝解。泉者，喻於內等淨支。水軸者，謂水傍流出。水索者：謂水上涌出。此二種喻，如其次第，顯示喜、樂滋潤等言，如前解釋。無不充滿者，當知喻於無間相應。又於第三喻有差別。如嗢鉢羅等離喜之樂，彼相應法及所依身，當知亦爾。水喻離喜無尋伺定。喜發踊躍，由無彼故，喻花胎藏沒在水中。
items.en: Again, for the second there is a difference in the simile. The mountain illustrates the concentration without applied and sustained thought; its peak illustrates the second dhyāna's single-flavoured conviction towards its object, free of applied and sustained thought; the spring illustrates the limb of inner clarity; the water flowing out sideways and the water welling up illustrate, in order, the drenching by joy and by bliss, as explained before; and "nothing left unfilled" illustrates the uninterrupted correspondence [with the body]. Again, for the third there is a difference. As the utpala lotus and the rest [are soaked] in the bliss apart from joy, so too are its associated factors and the body that supports them; the water illustrates the concentration apart from joy, free of applied and sustained thought, and, because joy's leaping exultation is absent, it is illustrated by the flower-buds submerged beneath the water.

items.zh: 又於第四喻有差別。清淨心者，謂與捨念清淨相應。超過下地諸災患故。鮮白者，謂性是善。自地煩惱無愛味故。何故復以長者為喻？謂彼所作皆審悉故，不放逸故，思惟籌量觀察勝故，於增減門無不知故。證得清淨第四靜慮者，亦復如是。凡有所為審諦圓滿，無諸放逸，於一切義無不了知，其性捷利。八經九經以為喻者，由堅緻故，顯蚊虻等不能侵損。首足皆覆者，若有二失，容可侵損。謂衣薄故，有露處故。今此顯示二失俱無。此定亦爾，其心清淨鮮白周遍，一切散動所不能侵；堪忍寒暑乃至他所呵叱惡言，及內身中種種苦受。
items.en: Again, for the fourth there is a difference. "A purified mind" means associated with pure equanimity-and-mindfulness, having transcended the lower grounds' calamities; "bright-white" means its nature is wholesome, with no relish for its own ground's afflictions. … This concentration too is such: its mind pure, bright-white, and all-pervading, which no scattering can invade; it endures cold and heat, and even others' scolding and abuse, and every kind of painful feeling within the body.

blocks.text: Today's reading contains four of the most beautiful similes in Buddhist literature, from the sūtras: the bliss of each dhyāna pervading the body like water in a bath-ball, a spring-fed lake, lotuses in water, and a white cloth wrapping the whole body. Read them slowly; they are meant to be contemplated.

A noble one verifies his own concentration by five knowledges: of its nature, of the person who has it, of its purity, of its fruit, and of entering and leaving it. Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the Tang commentator Wénbèi, maps them onto technical knowledges: dharma-knowledge, inferential knowledge, knowledge of exhaustion, knowledge of non-arising, and knowledge of others' minds. The point is that a noble practitioner does not need to guess: he knows what his concentration is, where it comes from, and where it leads.

"Joy-and-bliss born of seclusion drenches and pervades the body", as when a skilled bath attendant kneads bath-powder with water into a ball, moist through and through, with no part dry. Venerable Miào Jìng: "the fine bath-powder is probably something like soap." "Drenched" is by joy; "pervadingly drenched", by bliss. The first dhyāna's pleasure leaves no part of the body untouched.

subs.head: The second limb: a spring-fed lake

blocks.text: The second dhyāna's joy-and-bliss born of concentration is like a lake on a mountain fed by a spring from below, so that cool water fills it with nothing coming from outside. Master Cháng Bǎi: the mountain means height, since the second dhyāna rises above the first; the "water-axle" is the spring flowing sideways, thick as a cart axle. Joy now arises from within, not from seclusion from something outside.

The third dhyāna's bliss without joy is like blue, red, and white lotuses born, grown, and remaining entirely under water, soaked from root to tip. The swimmer is fully submerged (Day 79): no more bobbing of joy, only still bliss throughout.

subs.head: The fourth limb: a white cloth

blocks.text: The fourth dhyāna's purified equanimity and mindfulness is like a person wrapped head to foot in a clean white cloth: "pervading the whole body with a pure, bright mind". Not pleasure now, but purity and clarity, everywhere at once.

Notice the progression: kneaded water, upwelling water, still water, and then no water at all, only a clean cloth. Each image is quieter than the last, matching the dhyānas' movement from joy to bliss to equanimity. The fifth limb, tomorrow, is the "**reviewing mark**", seeing the concentration clearly from outside, which is what makes this five-limbed concentration "noble": insight into the very states one enjoys.

quiz.q: The five noble knowledges — how does Master Cháng Bǎi, citing Wenbei, map them?
options: self-nature knowledge is dharma-knowledge; person, inferential; purity, exhaustion; fruit, non-arising; entering-exiting, path-knowledge
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Wenbei says: self-nature knowledge is dharma-knowledge; person-knowledge inferential knowledge; purity-knowledge exhaustion-knowledge; fruit-knowledge non-arising knowledge; entering-exiting knowledge path-knowledge." The text names the five.

quiz.q: In the first limb, what do "drenched" and "pervadingly drenched" refer to?
options: drenched by joy; pervadingly drenched by bliss
quiz.why: "'Joy-and-bliss born of seclusion' is the joy-and-bliss included in the first-dhyāna ground. 'Drenched' means moistened by joy; 'pervadingly drenched' means moistened by bliss." Master Cháng Bǎi: like a farmer irrigating a field in four stages.

quiz.q: In the bath simile, what does Venerable Miào Jìng say the "fine bath-powder" is?
options: probably something like soap, for cleansing the body
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "The fine bath-powder is probably something like soap, used to cleanse the body." The text: it represents what conforms to the thought of renunciation; the water, the purifying path. Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the *Lüezuan*: it's the uninterrupted path.

quiz.q: The second limb uses a mountain. What does Master Cháng Bǎi say it illustrates?
options: height — the second dhyāna, free of applied thought, rises above the first
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The mountain means height — the second dhyāna, a concentration free of applied and sustained thought, rises above the first." The text: the peak is single-flavoured conviction; the spring, inner clarity.

quiz.q: In the second-limb simile, how does Master Cháng Bǎi explain the "water-axle" (水軸)?
options: the spring flowing sideways, thick as a cart axle — the second-dhyāna practitioner soaked by joy
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "水軸 means the spring flowing out sideways, thick as a cart axle — the successful second-dhyāna practitioner's body and mind moistened by joy." The text: sideways flow and upwelling show, in order, drenching by joy and by bliss.
